title: Titans for Continual Learning: Neural Long-Term Memory as a Catastrophic Forgetting Mitigation Mechanism
description: Problem: Continual learning systems suffer from catastrophic forgetting when sequentially trained on new tasks, as gradient updates overwrite previously learned representations. Existing solutions (EWC, replay buffers, progressive networks) either impose computational overhead or require storing raw data. The Titans architecture's neural long-term memory module—which learns to selectively memorize and forget information at test time—presents a natural inductive bias for continual learning that has not been explored. Proposed Method: We adapt the Titans memory module as a task-agnostic persistent memory store in a continual learning framework. Specifically, we (1) treat each task's learned memory state as a compressible episodic summary, (2) introduce a memory consolidation objective that penalizes high-surprise updates to previously memorized representations (analogous to synaptic consolidation), and (3) leverage the test-time learning capability to rapidly adapt to new tasks while preserving past memory via a selective write-gating mechanism tied to task boundaries. No raw replay data is stored. Experiments: We evaluate on Split-CIFAR-100, Permuted-MNIST, and a novel long-horizon NLP continual benchmark across 50 sequential tasks. Metrics include backward transfer, forward transfer, and memory footprint. We compare against EWC, PackNet, DER++, and Mamba-based recurrent baselines, expecting Titans to achieve superior backward transfer with minimal overhead.

title: Titans for Code: Long-Term Memory Architectures for Repository-Scale Program Understanding
description: Problem: Modern LLMs struggle with repository-scale code understanding, where relevant context (function definitions, class hierarchies, API contracts) is scattered across thousands of files far beyond practical context windows. description:

These three memory streams are fused via a modified Titans MAC (Memory as Context) variant with cross-modal attention gates that selectively retrieve relevant biological context. The neural memory is pre-trained with a masked token objective over UniRef90, then fine-tuned on structure-function prediction.

Experiments: (1) Zero-shot protein function prediction on SwissProt benchmarks vs. ESM-2 and Mamba baselines; (2) Long-range genomic regulatory element prediction on ENCODE data (up to 1M context); (3) Needle-in-haystack retrieval of functional residues across full proteome sequences; (4) Ablations comparing memory module contributions. title: Hierarchical Titans: Multi-Scale Neural Memory for Structured Document Understanding
description:

Proposed Method: We introduce Hierarchical Titans (H-Titans), which augments the Titans architecture with multiple neural memory modules operating at different temporal scales. A token-level memory captures local syntactic patterns, a sentence-level memory aggregates over detected clause boundaries (using lightweight boundary detection), and a document-level memory compresses section-scale semantics. Each memory module uses the Titans surprise-based update rule but with dynamically adjusted learning rates proportional to detected boundary salience. A learned gating mechanism routes attention queries to the appropriate memory hierarchy.

Experiments: (1) Long-document QA benchmarks (SCROLLS, QuALITY, ContractNLI) measuring multi-hop reasoning across document sections. (2) Code completion on repository-level tasks (CrossCodeEval) requiring cross-file context. (3) Scientific literature comprehension requiring citation-level reasoning. No explicit replay buffer is maintained—memory compression handles storage implicitly. Comparisons against EWC, PackNet, DER++, and ER-ACE. Metrics: average accuracy, backward/forward transfer, memory footprint, and task inference accuracy.

title: TitanMed: Adaptive Long-Term Memory Architectures for Longitudinal Electronic Health Record Modeling
description: Problem: Electronic health records (EHRs) contain patient histories spanning years or decades, but existing transformer-based clinical models are constrained to short context windows, forcing truncation of critical historical events. Recurrent alternatives compress history too aggressively, losing rare but clinically decisive events (e.g., prior adverse drug reactions, genetic test results). Titans' neural long-term memory module—which selectively memorizes salient historical context while maintaining fast inference—offers a compelling solution for longitudinal patient modeling. Proposed Method: We adapt the Titans MAC (Memory as a Context) architecture for EHR sequential modeling by (1) designing a clinical surprise metric that prioritizes memorization of rare, high-acuity events (ICU admissions, unusual lab values) over routine vitals, (2) incorporating structured EHR ontologies (ICD/SNOMED codes) into the memory addressing mechanism, and (3) introducing a memory decay schedule aligned with clinical recency bias. Planned Experiments: We evaluate on MIMIC-IV and PhysioNet datasets across three tasks: 30-day readmission prediction, in-hospital mortality, and medication recommendation. We compare against GPT-2 fine-tuned variants, Mamba-based clinical models, and Longformer. Ablations examine memory capacity, surprise-based retention vs. uniform retention, and performance as history length grows beyond 5 years, demonstrating that adaptive long-term memory improves both accuracy and calibration on rare critical events.

title: Titans for Continual Learning: Neural Long-Term Memory as a Catastrophic Forgetting Mitigation Mechanism
description: Problem: Continual learning systems suffer from catastrophic forgetting when neural networks are sequentially trained on new tasks, as gradient updates overwrite previously learned representations. Existing remedies (replay buffers, regularization, progressive networks) introduce significant memory or computational overhead. The Titans architecture's neural long-term memory module—designed to persistently memorize historical context at test time—presents an underexplored opportunity for naturally mitigating forgetting without explicit replay. Proposed Method: We adapt the Titans memory module as a persistent task-knowledge store in continual learning settings. Specifically, we introduce a 'task-selective memory gating' mechanism that learns to write new task knowledge to orthogonal memory subspaces while preserving existing memory traces via a surprise-weighted write gate. At inference, a learned memory retrieval head selectively reads task-relevant knowledge. Unlike standard replay, no raw data is stored; the compressed neural memory implicitly encodes task statistics. We also propose a memory consolidation phase between tasks that compresses redundant memory entries. Experiments: We evaluate on Split-CIFAR-100, Permuted-MNIST, and Split-Omniglot benchmarks against EWC, PackNet, DER++, and vanilla transformers. We measure backward transfer, forward transfer, average accuracy, and memory footprint scaling with number of tasks (up to 50). Ablations isolate contributions of orthogonal subspace writing vs. surprise gating.
